notes.title: The big picture: one message, several jobs
notes.body:
Imagine sending a letter across the world. You write the letter (**Application**), put it in an envelope addressed to a specific person (**Transport**), add a street address and zip code so the post office can route it (**Network**), hand it to a mail truck operating on a local street (**Data Link**), and the truck moves physically across paved roads (**Physical**). 

Computer networking uses this exact divided approach called **Layering**. Instead of building one giant system that handles everything from web page code down to copper electricity, the process is divided into separate, independent layers.
notes.remember: Remember: Each layer does one part of delivery. The letter analogy is a memory aid, not an exact description of every protocol.

notes.title: What is Layering & Why is it Used?
notes.body:
* **Layering** means dividing the complex task of networking into separate, stacked levels, where each level has one specific job.
* **Why it’s useful**:
  1. **Modularity / Layer Independence**: You can upgrade or change one layer (e.g., changing the local connection from Wi-Fi to Ethernet, which changes Physical and Data Link details) without redesigning your web browser at the Application layer.
  2. **Simplicity & Troubleshooting**: It breaks a massive problem into manageable parts, making it easy to isolate where a network failure is happening.
  3. **Standardization**: Allows hardware and software from hundreds of different vendors to work together seamlessly.
notes.remember: Remember: Each layer has its own job. You can investigate one job without having to understand the whole network at once.

notes.title: The TCP/IP Model (How the Internet Actually Works)
notes.body:
Your course teaches a **five-layer TCP/IP model**. Other references group Data Link and Physical into one Link layer and therefore show four. Use five for this guide.

| Layer # | Layer Name | Primary Function | Key Data Unit (PDU) | Key Address Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **5** | **Application** | Provides network services directly to end-user software (e.g., web browsers, email clients). | Data / Message | Domain Names / URLs |
| **4** | **Transport** | Manages end-to-end communication between applications; handles segmentation, reassembly, and port numbers. | Segment (TCP) / Datagram (UDP) | Port Numbers (e.g., Port 80 for HTTP) |
| **3** | **Network (IP)** | Handles logical IP addressing and routes packets across multiple interconnected networks. | IP Packet | IP Address (e.g., `173.245.63.1`) |
| **2** | **Data Link** | Transfers frames across a single local link/hop between adjacent devices using physical hardware addresses. | Frame | MAC Address (e.g., `00-15-C5-57-1D-1A`) |
| **1** | **Physical** | Transmits raw binary bits (0s and 1s) as electrical voltage, light pulses, or radio waves over a medium. | Bits | None |
notes.remember: Remember: Think top to bottom: application data, transport delivery, IP routing, local frames, then physical signals.

notes.title: The OSI Model (The Theoretical Blueprint)
notes.body:
* **OSI Model (Open Systems Interconnection)**: A 7-layer reference model developed to standardize networking so equipment from any vendor could interoperate. While TCP/IP is what we actually use, OSI is the standard theoretical blueprint.
* **The 7 Layers (Top-to-Bottom)**:
  1. **Application**: Network services for software.
  2. **Presentation**: Data formatting, compression, and encryption/decryption.
  3. **Session**: Establishes, manages, and terminates communication sessions between hosts.
  4. **Transport**: End-to-end communication between application processes. TCP adds reliable delivery and flow control; not every transport protocol guarantees these.
  5. **Network**: IP addressing and global routing.
  6. **Data Link**: Local node-to-node framing and error detection.
  7. **Physical**: Hardware signaling and bit transmission.
* **Mnemonic to Remember 7 to 1**: **A**ll **P**eople **S**eem **T**o **N**eed **D**ata **P**rocessing.
* **Mnemonic to Remember 1 to 7**: **P**lease **D**o **N**ot **T**hrow **S**ausage **P**izza **A**way.
notes.remember: Remember: OSI separates seven jobs. Presentation changes the data’s format; Session manages the conversation.

notes.title: Encapsulation vs. Decapsulation
notes.body:
* **Encapsulation (Sending side)**: The process of wrapping data in headers (and sometimes trailers) as it moves down through the layers.
  * *Analogy*: You write a letter (**Data**), put it in a box (**TCP Segment**), place that box inside an Amazon brown box with an IP shipping label (**IP Packet**), and load that box onto a delivery truck (**Ethernet Frame**).
* **Decapsulation (Receiving side)**: The reverse process where the receiving device strips off headers layer by layer as data moves up the stack.
* **Remember**: A router removes the incoming link-layer frame and builds a new frame for the next link. Ordinary switches do not rewrite the frame at every switch hop. IP source and destination addresses usually remain the same without address translation, but IP headers are not completely unchanged: routers reduce TTL and update the IPv4 header checksum.
notes.remember: Remember: Sending adds wrapping; receiving removes it. A router builds new link-layer wrapping for the next link.

notes.title: Vocabulary: Computer Network Authorities
notes.body:
Standards ensure devices worldwide speak the same language:
* **IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)**: *"Cables & Wi-Fi people."* Sets LAN and physical/data-link standards (e.g., Ethernet = `IEEE 802.3`, Wi-Fi = `IEEE 802.11`).
* **IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force)**: *"Internet protocol people."* Creates TCP/IP stack standards like HTTP, TCP, IP, and DNS.
* **ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers)**: *"Domain names boss."* Coordinates the global domain-name system and root-zone policy; it does not operate every DNS root server.
* **IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)**: *"Numbers and ports clerk."* Coordinates global IP-number resources and protocol-parameter registries, including port numbers. The IANA functions are performed by Public Technical Identifiers, an ICANN affiliate; regional registries handle regional allocations.
* **ITU (International Telecommunication Union)**: *"Global telecom referee."* UN agency that sets global WAN and carrier telecom standards.
* **TIA (Telecommunications Industry Association)**: *"Building cabling people."* Writes commercial cabling standards (e.g., TIA-568) for building wiring.
notes.remember: Remember: IEEE is the Ethernet/Wi-Fi standards group; IETF is the Internet-protocol standards group.

notes.title: Primary Responsibility & Physical Media
notes.body:
* **Primary Function**: To convert raw binary bits (0s and 1s) into physical signals (electricity, light, radio waves) and send them through a medium.
* **Physical Medium**: The physical path that carries a signal between devices.
* **Required Properties of a Good Medium**: Must effectively conduct signals, support required data rates (bandwidth), transmit over desired distances, resist environmental noise/interference, and be cost-effective to install.
notes.remember: Remember: Bits are information. Signals are the physical form that lets those bits travel.

notes.title: Copper Cabling: UTP Categories
notes.body:
* **UTP (Unshielded Twisted Pair)**: Copper cabling containing pairs of insulated wires twisted around each other. 
  * **Why twist the wires?** Twisting helps reduce electromagnetic interference (EMI) and crosstalk between pairs. Cable performance depends on the complete cable design and installation, not only how tightly it is twisted.
  * **STP (Shielded Twisted Pair)**: Includes an extra foil shield around wires for high-noise industrial environments.
* **Twisted-pair cable categories and common Ethernet limits** (Cat 8 is shielded, not UTP):
  * **Cat 5e (Enhanced)**: Up to **1 Gbps** (Gigabit Ethernet).
  * **Cat 6**: Up to **1 Gbps** (and 10 Gbps over short distances up to 55m).
  * **Cat 6a (Augmented)**: Full **10 Gbps** up to 100 meters.
  * **Cat 8**: **25 Gbps to 40 Gbps** over short distances (30m, ideal for Data Centers).
* **Baseband vs. Broadband**:
  * **Baseband**: Uses the entire cable bandwidth to transmit **one single digital signal** at a time (e.g., Ethernet).
  * **Broadband**: Divides cable bandwidth into multiple channels to send **multiple signals simultaneously** (e.g., Cable TV).
notes.remember: Remember: Twists reduce interference. Choose cable by the required speed and distance, not just its category number.

notes.title: Fiber Optics: Single-Mode vs. Multi-Mode
notes.body:
**Optical fiber** is a thin strand of glass that conducts light using **Total Internal Reflection**. Light strikes the boundary between the inner core and outer cladding at an angle greater than the critical angle, trapping the light inside the core so it travels vast distances without escaping.

Why is Fiber better than Copper? Fiber can support high bandwidth and long links and is immune to electromagnetic interference. Reach still depends on the fiber, optics and data rate; sufficiently long links need amplification or regeneration.

| Feature | Single-Mode Fiber (SMF) | Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Diameter** | Very small (**9 µm**) | Larger (**50 – 62.5 µm**) |
| **Light Source** | Laser | LED or laser, including VCSELs in many modern links |
| **Distance** | **Very Long Distances** (miles/km across cities/oceans) | **Short Distances** (inside a building or data center) |
| **Cost** | More expensive optics/transceivers | Lower cost optics |
notes.remember: Remember: A fiber guides light through its core. Single-mode usually suits longer links; multimode usually suits shorter ones.

notes.title: Signaling & Modulation
notes.body:
Computers cannot transmit abstract concepts of 0 and 1 directly; they must convert binary data into physical signals.

* **Properties of a Good Signal**: Easily detectable by receiver, resistant to noise, bandwidth efficient, and supports multiplexing.
* **Modulation Types**:
  * **AM (Amplitude Modulation)**: Varies the height/strength of the wave. Simple, but highly sensitive to noise.
  * **FM (Frequency Modulation)**: Varies the frequency (cycles per second) of the wave. Good noise resistance.
  * **PM (Phase Modulation)**: Varies the starting position/angle (phase) of the wave.
  * **QAM (Quadrature Amplitude Modulation)**: Combines **AM + PM** simultaneously. It packs multiple bits into every signal state, making it extremely **bandwidth efficient** (used in Wi-Fi and 5G), but higher-order QAM is sensitive to channel noise.
notes.remember: Remember: Amplitude means wave strength, frequency means cycles per second, and phase means position in the cycle. QAM changes amplitude and phase together.

notes.title: Mathematical Limits & Multiplexing
notes.body:
* **Shannon-Hartley Theorem**: Calculates the theoretical capacity for a bandwidth-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise (Channel Capacity C in bits per second) over a noisy channel:
**C = B × log₂(1 + S/N)**
  * B = Channel Bandwidth in Hertz (Hz).
  * S/N = Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), expressed as a linear power ratio, not decibels.
  * *Takeaway*: Higher bandwidth (B) or cleaner signals (higher S/N) yield higher data capacity (C).

* **Multiplexing**: Combining multiple separate signals onto a single shared physical medium to save cabling costs.
  * **FDM (Frequency Division Multiplexing)**: Divides the channel into different **frequency bands** (like tuning radio stations or low/high pitches). Separates signals by frequency; those carriers can carry analog or digital information.
  * **TDM (Time Division Multiplexing)**: Devices take **turns in time slots** to send data over the full frequency. Common in digital systems; its defining feature is division by time.
notes.remember: Remember: Multiplexing lets several conversations share one medium. FDM separates frequencies; TDM separates turns in time.

notes.title: Primary Functions of Data Link Layer
notes.body: Operating across a single local link/hop, the Data Link layer creates **Frames**, handles hardware addressing (**MAC addresses**), detects transmission errors (**CRC**), and regulates media access (**CSMA/CD**).
notes.remember: Remember: Data Link organizes local delivery into frames. Physical carries the signals underneath those frames.

notes.title: Ethernet Operation & CSMA/CD
notes.body:
On traditional shared Ethernet, other connected interfaces can hear a transmission. A unicast frame is addressed to one interface; an Ethernet broadcast frame is addressed to all interfaces in the broadcast domain. Modern switched Ethernet does not send every known unicast frame to every workstation.

When multiple devices share a medium, they can transmit at the same time, causing a **Collision**. This applies to shared half-duplex Ethernet; modern full-duplex switched links do not use CSMA/CD. Shared Ethernet resolves this using **CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)**:
1. **Carrier Sense**: Listen to the wire first ("listen before speaking").
2. **Multiple Access**: If the wire is quiet, transmit.
3. **Collision Detect**: If two devices transmit simultaneously, they detect the voltage spike collision.
4. **Backoff**: Both devices immediately stop, send a jam signal, wait a random fraction of a second (exponential backoff), and retransmit.
notes.remember: Remember: Listen first. If a collision happens on a shared half-duplex link, stop, signal the collision, wait a random time and retry.

notes.title: Ethernet Frame Structure & Math
notes.body:
The maximum **ordinary untagged Ethernet frame** in this guide is **1,518 bytes**; tagged and jumbo frames differ (excluding the 8-byte Preamble and Start Frame Delimiter):

**1518 bytes = 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS**

* **Preamble + SFD (8 Bytes)**: Synchronizes clock timing between sender and receiver.
* **Destination MAC Address (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical address of receiving device.
* **Source MAC Address (6 Bytes / 48 bits)**: Physical address of sending device.
* **Type/Length (2 Bytes)**: Identifies the layer-3 protocol inside (e.g., IPv4).
* **Payload Data**: The encapsulated IP packet (46 to 1500 Bytes).
* **FCS (Frame Check Sequence - 4 Bytes)**: Contains a **CRC-32 (Cyclic Redundancy Check)** used to detect corruption. A failed check indicates an error. A passing check means no error was detected, not proof that every bit must be correct.
notes.remember: Remember: For an ordinary untagged frame: 14 + 1500 + 4 = 1518 bytes. The preamble and SFD are outside that count.

notes.title: MAC Address Structure & Hexadecimal Conversions
notes.body:
A traditional Ethernet **MAC address** is 48 bits (6 bytes). Interfaces often have a factory-assigned address, but software can also set or randomize MAC addresses; they are not necessarily permanent.
* **First 24 bits**: **OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier)**—assigned by IEEE to the manufacturer (e.g., Cisco, Broadcom).
* **Last 24 bits**: Unique extension/serial number assigned by the manufacturer.

#### Number Conversion Practice for the Exam:
1. **Binary to Decimal**: Sum the positional powers of 2 (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1) where a 1 appears:
**10101101₂ = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 173₁₀**
2. **Binary to Hexadecimal**: Group the 8 bits into two 4-bit nibbles (8, 4, 2, 1):
**1010 1111₂ → 1010 = A and 1111 = F → AF₁₆**
notes.remember: Remember: A MAC address has six bytes. For number conversions, add binary place values or group bits into fours for hex.

notes.title: Network Hardware & Topologies
notes.body:
* **Hub vs. Switch**:
  * **Hub (Layer 1)**: Dumb multiport repeater. A signal received on one port is repeated to the other ports. Creates a single large collision domain.
  * **Switch (Layer 2)**: Intelligent device. Reads incoming Source MAC addresses to dynamically build a **MAC Address Table** (`[MAC Address → Switch Port]`). For a known unicast destination, forwards to the learned destination port. Broadcasts and unknown unicasts are flooded to other eligible ports in the same VLAN.
* **Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)**:
  * **Problem**: Redundant links between switches create switching **loops**, causing frames to circulate endlessly and crash the network.
  * **Solution**: Invented by **Radia Perlman**, STP dynamically blocks redundant paths to create a single loop-free tree structure, automatically unblocking backup paths if a link fails.
* **Topologies**:
  * **Star**: All devices connect to a central switch. **Dominant topology today** because it offers superior fault tolerance, easy maintenance, and security.
  * **Bus**: Single central backbone cable with terminators at both ends.
  * **Ring**: Devices connected in a closed circle.
  * **Mesh**: Devices have redundant connections to each other (Full Mesh or Partial Mesh).
notes.remember: Remember: A hub repeats signals. A switch learns which MAC addresses are on which ports. STP prevents loops when switches have redundant links.

notes.title: Why do we need IP Addresses when we already have MAC Addresses?
notes.body:
* **MAC Address (Layer 2)**: Link-layer interface address; often factory-assigned but not necessarily permanent. It only works for **local hop-by-hop delivery** within a single network segment.
* **IP Address (Layer 3)**: Logical, hierarchical address that identifies the device’s network location for routing, not its physical geographic location across interconnected networks.
* **Layering Independence**: Allows you to replace a network card (changing the MAC address) without changing the computer's logical IP address or server configurations.
notes.remember: Remember: MAC helps with the next local delivery. IP helps routers choose a path across networks.

notes.title: IP Address Structure & Math Rules
notes.body:
An IPv4 address consists of **32 bits** divided into two parts: `[Network Portion | Host Portion]`.

#### Exam Math Problems:
1. **How many objects can be labeled with n bits?**
**Number of unique labels = 2ⁿ**
   * *Example*: With 10 bits, 2^10 = 1,024 unique objects can be labeled.
   * *Example*: To label 200 objects, find the smallest power of 2 that covers 200: 2^7 = 128 (too small), 2^8 = 256 (sufficient). Answer = **8 bits**.

2. **CIDR Subnet Calculations (Classless Inter-Domain Routing)**:
   * Classful addressing (Classes A, B, C) was rigid and wasted millions of addresses. CIDR replaced it by allowing variable prefix lengths using slash notation (e.g., `/17`).
   * *Exam Problem*: For network `73.5.0.0/17`:
     * Total IPv4 bits = 32.
     * Network bits = 17.
     * Host bits = 32 - 17 = **15 host bits**.
     * **Total IP Addresses**: 2^15 = **32,768  addresses**.
     * **Usable Host Addresses**: 2^15 - 2 = **32,766  usable hosts**.
     * *(Why subtract 2? We reserve the first address as the Network ID and the last address as the Subnet Broadcast Address)*.

The subtract-two rule is for traditional IPv4 subnets; /31 point-to-point links and /32 host routes are exceptions.
notes.remember: Remember: The slash number tells you how many bits are network bits. Subtract it from 32 to find the IPv4 host bits.

notes.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
notes.body:
* **IPv4**: **32 bits** long, written in 4 dotted-decimal octets (e.g., `192.168.1.1`). Yields ≈ 4.3  billion addresses, The address space is limited, and new-address allocation is constrained.
* **IPv6**: **128 bits** long, written in hexadecimal separated by colons. Yields 2^128 ≈ 3.4 × 10^38 addresses.
  * **Shortening Rules**:
    1. Omit leading zeros in any 16-bit block (`0011` → `11`, `0db8` → `db8`).
    2. Replace continuous blocks of zeros with a single double-colon `::` **(can only be done ONCE in an address)**.
    * *Example*: `2001:0db8:aaaa:0000:0000:0000:eeee:0001` shortens to `2001:db8:aaaa::eeee:1`.
notes.remember: Remember: IPv4 is 32 bits; IPv6 is 128. In IPv6, :: is a shortcut for consecutive zero groups and can appear only once.

notes.title: Routing, ICMP & IP Registries
notes.body:
* **Routing & Routing Tables**: Routing is the process of forwarding packets across networks. A **Routing Table** stores destination network prefixes, metrics/costs, and the next-hop router address.
* **ICMP Utilities (Internet Control Message Protocol)**: Used for diagnostic messages and status reporting:
  * **Ping**: Tests basic reachability to a target host via Echo Request/Reply.
  * **Traceroute**: Attempts to show successive router hops. Some routers do not reply, and paths can change.
  * **Pathping**: Combines ping and traceroute to measure packet loss and latency at each intermediate hop over time.
* **Regional Internet Registries (RIRs)**: Regional organizations (such as ARIN and RIPE NCC) that manage and distribute public IP address allocations regionally to prevent IP conflicts.
notes.remember: Remember: Ping asks for a reply. Traceroute explores the hops. Regional registries coordinate public address allocations.

notes.title: Network Design Goals & Phases
notes.body:
* **Primary Goal**: Meet current and future end-user needs using appropriate technology while **minimizing total costs** (initial setup + ongoing maintenance + cost of downtime).
* **Requirements Analysis Phase**: Gathering user counts, applications, physical locations, traffic volumes, and security/special device needs.
* **Logical Network Design**: A conceptual drawing/map showing network structure, subnets, IP ranges, device counts (desktops, servers, printers), and services (DNS, DHCP, firewalls) **without specifying vendor brand names**.
* **Physical Network Design**: Translates the logical design into explicit physical hardware specs, media types (Cat6a vs Fiber), specific switch models, and router configurations.
notes.remember: Remember: First learn what users need. Then plan the network, choose equipment and account for ongoing costs.

notes.title: Structured Cabling Components
notes.body:
Building cabling is organized into standardized facilities:
* **Demarc (Demarcation Point)**: The exact physical point where the Telecom ISP’s network ends and the customer’s internal building network begins.
* **MDF (Main Distribution Frame)**: The primary central telecommunications room housing core switches, main patch panels, and ISP handoffs.
* **IDF (Intermediate Distribution Frame)**: Secondary wiring closets located on individual floors that connect local devices and uplink back to the MDF.
* **Horizontal Cabling**: Cabling running from floor telecommunications rooms (IDFs) out to work area wall outlets. **For a typical structured copper channel: 90 meters of permanent cabling + 10 meters of patch cords = 100 meters. Specific standards, including Cat 8, have different limits**.
* **Vertical / Backbone Cabling**: High-capacity backbone links (typically fiber) connecting the MDF across floors to IDFs or adjacent buildings.
notes.remember: Remember: Horizontal goes to work areas; backbone joins telecommunications spaces. MDF is the main distribution point and IDFs serve other areas.

notes.title: Data Center & Campus Architectures
notes.body:
* **Data Center Leaf-Spine Architecture**: Every **Leaf switch** connects to every **Spine switch**. Provides multiple predictable paths between servers. Capacity and whether the network is non-blocking depend on link speeds and oversubscription.
* **Campus 3-Tier Architecture**: Organizes large multi-building networks into three distinct layers:

```
   [ Core Layer ]         <-- High-speed Backbone (fast transport)
         |
[ Distribution Layer ]    <-- Policy, Routing between VLANs, Firewalls
         |
  [ Access Layer ]        <-- Connects End-User PCs & Workstations
```

1. **Core Layer**: The fast network backbone. Prioritizes fast, reliable transport between distribution blocks; exact policy placement depends on the design.
2. **Distribution Layer**: Aggregates access networks and commonly handles inter-subnet routing and policy. Firewalls, authentication and QoS placement depend on the design.
3. **Access Layer**: Provides work-area ports to end users; contains user switches/hubs organizing building devices into local network segments.
* **Enterprise Network**: Connects geographically scattered campus networks over Wide Area Networks (WANs) managed by service providers.
notes.remember: Remember: Access connects users, Distribution brings access networks together, and Core provides the fast backbone.

notes.title: Network Maintenance & SNMP
notes.body:
* **Maintenance Activities**: Ongoing inspection, testing, hardware replacement, and software patching to maintain service availability. Vulnerability tools such as **Nessus** can help identify missing patches and other issues; they do not replace the patching process.
* **SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol)**: A protocol that allows a central Management Station to monitor and control network hardware remotely:
  * **Agent**: Software running inside routers, switches, and servers.
  * **MIB (Management Information Base)**: A structured definition of managed objects, such as counters and temperature readings. An agent exposes the actual values; the MIB describes what those objects mean.
  * **GET Command**: Management station asks the agent for managed-object values to retrieve statistics (e.g., CPU usage, toner percentage).
  * **SET Command**: Management station asks the agent to change an authorized writable managed object (e.g., shutting down a port, changing routing).
notes.remember: Remember: The manager asks; the agent answers. The MIB describes the information available through SNMP.

notes.title: Standards Development Process
notes.body:
How standard protocols (like Wi-Fi `802.11ax` or `TCP/IP`) are created:
1. An expert lead organization (like IEEE or IETF) identifies a industry need and forms a Working Group.
2. Requirements are published.
3. Technology companies submit proposed solutions.
4. Proposals undergo technical review, revision and approval. Procedures differ: IEEE uses ballots, while IETF working groups seek rough consensus rather than a simple majority vote.
notes.remember: Remember: A standard is a shared rule. Experts propose, discuss, revise and approve it so different products can work together.

notesQuestions.q: Why can a browser keep working when its local connection changes from Wi-Fi to Ethernet?
notesQuestions.answer: Layering separates application services from local-link details.
options: Layering separates application services from local-link details.
Every layer performs exactly the same function.
The browser must use the same radio signals as Ethernet.

notes-big-picture.title: Following one message
notes-big-picture.context: A network lets devices exchange information. Sending a message needs several jobs: prepare the data, identify the receiving application, find the destination network, cross the next local link, and transmit signals.
notes-big-picture.analogy: Like a delivery service: the letter, recipient, route, local delivery vehicle and road each play a different part.
notes-big-picture.example: You open a web page. Application protocols request it; Transport communicates between processes; IP routes packets; Data Link carries local frames; Physical transmits signals.

notes-1-1.title: Why networking is divided into layers
notes-1-1.context: In Chapter 1, a layer means one set of responsibilities in communication. The layers work together through defined interfaces. This makes a large system easier to build and troubleshoot.
notes-1-1.analogy: A restaurant separates taking orders, cooking and delivery. A new delivery vehicle does not require rewriting the menu.
notes-1-1.example: A browser can still request the same page after you change from Wi-Fi to Ethernet. The local connection changes; the browser’s network service can remain the same.

notes-1-2.title: The five jobs in your TCP/IP model
notes-1-2.context: Your course uses five layers. Application supplies network services. Transport connects application processes. Network chooses routes using IP. Data Link handles a local frame. Physical carries bits as signals.
notes-1-2.analogy: Think of delivery instructions: what to send, which recipient process, which network, the next local delivery, and the physical journey.
notes-1-2.example: A packet crossing several routers needs IP routing. Each individual local link uses a frame and physical signals. The five-layer course model separates those jobs. A Transport port number identifies the receiving application endpoint; for example, HTTP commonly uses port 80.

notes-1-3.title: Why OSI has seven layers
notes-1-3.context: Chapter 1 compares two ways of organizing network functions. OSI has seven layers. Its Presentation layer handles representation, such as formatting and encryption; Session manages conversations. TCP/IP groups these upper responsibilities under Application.
notes-1-3.analogy: OSI gives three separate desks to application services, formatting and conversation management. TCP/IP groups those desks into one upper department.
notes-1-3.example: OSI top to bottom: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Your five-layer TCP/IP list omits separate Presentation and Session entries.

notes-1-4.title: Wrapping and unwrapping data
notes-1-4.context: Encapsulation means adding control information around data as it travels down the sending stack. Decapsulation removes that wrapping as the receiver processes it up the stack.
notes-1-4.analogy: A letter goes into an addressed envelope, then into a local delivery container. Each wrapper helps with a different part of delivery.
notes-1-4.example: A router takes a packet out of its incoming frame, updates forwarding-related IP information, then builds a frame for the next link. The IP header is not completely unchanged.

notes-1-5.title: Who writes the shared rules?
notes-1-5.context: In Chapter 1, network authorities are organizations with different jobs. IEEE develops Ethernet and Wi-Fi standards. IETF develops Internet protocol standards. ICANN coordinates naming, and IANA coordinates shared number and parameter registries. TIA develops commercial building-cabling standards. ITU is the United Nations agency for international telecommunications.
notes-1-5.analogy: People agree on road signs so drivers from different towns understand them. Standards help devices made by different companies understand one another.
notes-1-5.example: For the paired question: LAN/WLAN standards → IEEE; Internet protocol standards → IETF. These are groups of people and organizations, not routers.

notes-2-1.title: Turning information into something that travels
notes-2-1.context: In Chapter 2, bits are the 0s and 1s that represent information. A signal is a physical change that carries those bits. The medium is the path: copper wire, optical fiber or radio through space.
notes-2-1.analogy: A spoken word is an idea carried by vibrations in air. Network data also needs a physical carrier.
notes-2-1.example: Copper uses electrical signals; fiber uses light; wireless uses radio. Choosing a medium means checking speed, distance, interference and cost.

notes-2-2.title: Choosing and understanding copper cable
notes-2-2.context: UTP means Unshielded Twisted Pair. Pairs of copper wires are twisted to reduce interference between signals. Cable categories describe performance requirements; distance and installation matter too.
notes-2-2.analogy: Two conversations in one room can interfere. Cable design helps a receiver distinguish its intended conversation.
notes-2-2.example: Common limits: Cat 5e supports 1 Gbps over 100 m; Cat 6a supports 10 Gbps over 100 m. Cat 8 supports 25/40 Gbps over shorter 30 m channels and is shielded. In the traditional cabling comparison, baseband uses an undivided signaling channel; broadband separates simultaneous signals into frequency channels.

notes-2-3.title: How fiber guides light
notes-2-3.context: Fiber carries light through a core surrounded by cladding. Total internal reflection keeps light guided in the core under the right conditions. Single-mode uses a smaller core; multimode allows multiple light paths.
notes-2-3.analogy: Imagine light following a carefully designed tunnel. Different paths can arrive at slightly different times, spreading a pulse.
notes-2-3.example: Single-mode core: about 9 µm, commonly for long links. Multimode core: 50 or 62.5 µm, commonly for shorter links. Reach depends on the optics and data rate, not just the name.

notes-2-4.title: How a wave carries different values
notes-2-4.context: Modulation changes a signal property to represent information. Amplitude is its strength; frequency is how often it repeats; phase is its position in a cycle. QAM changes amplitude and phase together.
notes-2-4.analogy: You could signal with a flashlight by changing its brightness or timing. The receiver needs to distinguish the changes.
notes-2-4.example: AM changes amplitude; FM changes frequency; PM changes phase. More QAM states can encode more bits per symbol, but closely spaced states are harder to distinguish in noise.

notes-2-5.title: Sharing a medium and understanding its limits
notes-2-5.context: Multiplexing lets several signals share one medium. FDM assigns frequency bands; TDM assigns time slots. Shannon’s formula relates theoretical capacity to channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio.
notes-2-5.analogy: FDM resembles different radio stations. TDM resembles people taking turns speaking into one microphone.
notes-2-5.example: For C = B × log₂(1 + S/N), if B = 1000 Hz and S/N = 3, then 1 + 3 = 4, log₂(4) = 2, and C = 2000 bits/s. S/N here is a linear ratio.

notes-3-1.title: Local delivery has its own wrapper
notes-3-1.context: In Chapter 3, Data Link handles communication over one local link. It organizes bits into a frame, uses link-layer addresses, manages access to the medium and detects errors.
notes-3-1.analogy: A local delivery label helps the next delivery step. It is different from the overall route across cities.
notes-3-1.example: An Ethernet frame includes destination and source MAC addresses, its payload and an error check. Physical sends the signals that carry the frame.

notes-3-2.title: Taking turns on shared Ethernet
notes-3-2.context: Older shared half-duplex Ethernet allows only one successful transmission at a time. CSMA/CD means listen first, transmit when idle, detect a collision, stop and back off randomly. Full-duplex switched Ethernet does not use collision detection.
notes-3-2.analogy: Two people start talking at once. They stop and wait different lengths of time so they do not immediately interrupt again.
notes-3-2.example: After a collision, devices send a jam signal and stop transmitting, then wait a random backoff interval before retrying.

notes-3-3.title: Reading an Ethernet frame
notes-3-3.context: A frame is a structured package with fields in a defined order. The addresses say who it is for and who sent it. The payload carries data. FCS is an error-detection value.
notes-3-3.analogy: An envelope has address fields and contents; the receiver needs to know which part is which.
notes-3-3.example: For an ordinary untagged maximum: 14-byte header + 1500-byte payload + 4-byte FCS = 1518 bytes. The 8-byte preamble/SFD is outside that total. A passing FCS check means no corruption was detected; it is not an absolute guarantee that every bit is correct.

notes-3-4.title: MAC addresses and number systems
notes-3-4.context: A traditional Ethernet MAC address is 48 bits, often written as six hexadecimal byte groups. Binary uses 0 and 1. Decimal uses 0–9. Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and A–F.
notes-3-4.analogy: Different number systems are different ways of writing the same quantity, like writing twelve versus 12.
notes-3-4.example: 10101101₂ has 1s at 128, 32, 8, 4 and 1: add them to get 173. For hex, 1010 = 10 = A and 1111 = 15 = F, so 1010 1111 = AF.

notes-3-5.title: Hubs, switches and network shapes
notes-3-5.context: A hub repeats incoming signals to other ports. A switch learns which MAC address is reachable through which port. Redundant switch links can create loops; STP blocks selected paths to prevent this.
notes-3-5.analogy: A hub resembles shouting to a room. A switch resembles a receptionist who knows which desk to contact; if it does not know, it asks more widely.
notes-3-5.example: Star has a central device; bus uses a shared cable; ring forms a circle; mesh has multiple interconnections. A switch floods unknown unicasts within the VLAN.

notes-4-1.title: Why a device needs IP as well as MAC
notes-4-1.context: Chapter 4 concerns delivery across interconnected networks. An IP address identifies a network location for routing. A MAC address identifies an interface for local-link delivery. Neither is a person’s street address.
notes-4-1.analogy: An overall destination gets the package to the right area; each local delivery stage needs its own instructions.
notes-4-1.example: When a router forwards to a new link, it builds a new local frame. Keeping local addressing separate lets the link technology change without redefining the whole IP system.

notes-4-2.title: A subnet is a group of addresses
notes-4-2.context: An IPv4 address has 32 bits grouped into four 8-bit octets. A subnet groups addresses that share a starting set of bits. The number after / says how many bits are this shared network prefix. The remaining bits vary within the group.
notes-4-2.analogy: Think of a street name shared by several houses and a house number that distinguishes them. The analogy helps explain shared versus varying parts.
notes-4-2.example: For /17: 8 bits in octet 1 + 8 in octet 2 + 1 in octet 3 = 17 network bits. There are 32 − 17 = 15 host bits. Use the decoder to build this one bit at a time.

notes-4-3.title: Reading IPv6 without getting lost
notes-4-3.context: IPv4 has 32 bits. IPv6 has 128 bits, normally eight groups of 16 bits written in hexadecimal. Leading zeros within a group can be omitted. One :: can stand for consecutive all-zero groups.
notes-4-3.analogy: The double colon is a space-saving placeholder. You must still be able to work out exactly how many groups it replaces.
notes-4-3.example: 2001:0db8:aaaa:0000:0000:0000:eeee:0001 becomes 2001:db8:aaaa::eeee:1. Five groups remain visible, so :: represents three zero groups.

notes-4-4.title: Routes, diagnostic tools and address registries
notes-4-4.context: Chapter 4 asks how packets find networks and who organizes public addresses. A router uses a routing table as a list of destination networks and forwarding directions. RIRs are organizations that register and distribute Internet-number resources in regions.
notes-4-4.analogy: A routing table is a signpost list. A registry is more like the office keeping address assignments organized; it is not a delivery vehicle.
notes-4-4.example: Allocation means giving an organization a block of addresses to manage or distribute. An ISP can receive a block and assign addresses to customers. RIR coordination helps prevent conflicting public allocations. For diagnostics, Ping asks for an echo reply, Traceroute explores successive hops, and Pathping measures loss and timing over time. A missing reply may be caused by filtering; it does not prove that traffic cannot pass.

notes-12-1.title: Design starts with the people using the network
notes-12-1.context: Chapter 12 is about planning a real organization’s network. First identify the end-users, applications, locations, traffic and security needs. Logical design plans the organization of the network. Physical design chooses actual equipment and cabling.
notes-12-1.analogy: Plan rooms and their purpose before buying the furniture. Otherwise you may buy equipment that does not fit the need.
notes-12-1.example: A school estimates student devices and application traffic, plans subnets and services, then selects switches and cables. Costs include maintenance and downtime, not just purchase price.

notes-12-2.title: How building wiring is organized
notes-12-2.context: Structured cabling organizes permanent wiring and connection points. The demarc is the provider/customer boundary. An MDF is a main distribution point; IDFs serve other areas. Horizontal cabling reaches work areas; backbone cabling joins telecommunications spaces.
notes-12-2.analogy: A main hallway connects smaller hallways, and those lead to rooms. This is an analogy for main distribution, intermediate areas and work-area connections.
notes-12-2.example: A desk connects through a wall outlet to a floor telecommunications room. Backbone cabling links that room to other distribution areas. A typical copper channel allows 90 m permanent cable plus 10 m patch cords.

notes-12-3.title: Where the campus Core layer fits
notes-12-3.context: In Chapter 12, Core means a role in a campus network design—not an OSI layer or the glass core of a fiber. The three campus roles are Access, Distribution and Core. Access connects users; Distribution groups access networks; Core links major network regions quickly and reliably.
notes-12-3.analogy: Access resembles neighborhood streets, Distribution resembles roads connecting neighborhoods, and Core resembles the main highway between larger areas.
notes-12-3.example: A campus has buildings A and B. Each has access switches for users and distribution switches for aggregation. Core connections carry traffic between those distribution areas. A data center uses another common design called leaf-spine: servers attach to leaf switches, and each leaf connects to every spine switch. This is different from the campus three-tier pattern.

notes-12-4.title: How an administrator checks devices remotely
notes-12-4.context: In Chapter 12, network maintenance means keeping service working. SNMP lets management software communicate with agents running on devices. A MIB describes the managed objects, such as an interface counter or temperature value.
notes-12-4.analogy: A manager asks a local assistant for a reading. A labeled form tells both of them what each field means.
notes-12-4.example: GET asks for a value. SET requests a change to an authorized writable object. The MIB is the definition of the objects, not a person doing the monitoring.

notes-12-5.title: Working groups are people making shared rules
notes-12-5.context: In Chapter 12, standards are written technical specifications that help products work together. A working group is a group of people—such as engineers and technical experts—who develop and review a specification. It is not a group of computers.
notes-12-5.analogy: People agree on the size and shape of a plug so independently made plugs and sockets can fit together.
notes-12-5.example: A group identifies a need, discusses requirements and proposals, revises a draft and seeks approval. IEEE uses ballots; IETF working groups seek rough consensus through discussion.
